rationale:
Today's long video is queue item #6, Serious Risks. It resubmits the 11-14 script that was held for a fact-check REVISE. That video never shipped, so it isn't a repeat angle. It's a broad searched question, and it absorbs the NAION label-change news while the body rests on the US labels. Search-demand quota is already met: Mounjaro vs Zepbound, Foundayo and Months 2–6 are all in the last 7 long videos, so a Lane A label explainer fits.

The NAION label change is peaking, but I kept it as one chapter. The radar says it's saturated as a standalone topic, and NAION, gallbladder and pancreatitis Shorts all ran within 30 days.

Shorts:
- **08:00:** a visible pen moment (a dropped pen) that hasn't run as a Short yet. Hair, bruise, pen blood, storage and flying are all within 30 days.
- **13:00:** a felt-symptom spin-off of L1: when stomach pain is ordinary and when it's a call-right-away sign.
- **20:00:** the holiday table. A contrarian-but-true "turkey first?" angle from the natural-GLP-1 pillar points to the Thanksgiving video. It avoids the full-fast, heartburn, drinks, greasy and leftovers angles already used.

Body systems are spread out: multi-system label warnings, the device, the stomach, and the appetite hormone. Pillars rotate, with one piece each. Retatrutide (pipeline), binge eating (semaglutide-only, caution), teens and the prebiotic soda pilot are skipped because they're study-led or off-playbook topics. Cost and coverage angles are banned.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) serious risks, how rare each one is, from the US labels: boxed thyroid C-cell warning (MTC/MEN 2), pancreatitis, gallbladder problems, low blood sugar with insulin or a sulfonylurea, kidney injury from fluid loss, severe allergic reactions, diabetic retinopathy (Mounjaro, type 2 diabetes), aspiration around anaesthesia, Suicidal Behavior and Ideation as the label names it, and the FDA's class-wide NAION eye warning
pieces.angle: Run the 11-14 script with every fix listed. Tag each warning with its label: Mounjaro only (diabetic retinopathy, in type 2 diabetes), Zepbound only (Suicidal Behavior and Ideation, said calmly, with crisis lines for the US, UK, Canada and Australia), or both. For post-marketing warnings (kidney injury from fluid loss, severe allergy, aspiration around anaesthesia), say 'reported after approval; the label gives no rate'. Present NAION as a class-wide FDA estimate: 6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years across 126 RCTs, a small number of events, not shown for tirzepatide alone. Sign: sudden, painless vision loss in one eye. Action: contact a clinician right away. Keep the scoped don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line, spoken and on screen.
pieces.why: Queue #6 and a broad searched question (Ro and WaPo safety pieces, NAION coverage). Absorbs the peaking NAION news into an evergreen, label-verifiable deep-dive. | fact-check: This is a resubmission, so we can do it once the 11-14 fixes are in. I checked the NAION facts: the FDA Drug Safety Communication on 9 Nov 2026 requires a class-wide NAION warning. Its meta-analysis covered 126 RCTs (134,253 patients, 288,879 person-years) and found 15 probable events: 6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years on GLP-1 RAs vs comparators. Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) is on the list of affected drugs. The rate is for the whole class, so it must not be given as a tirzepatide-only figure. Scope problem: the angle puts every warning under both labels, but they differ. Diabetic retinopathy is Mounjaro only, in type 2 diabetes. 'Suicidal Behavior and Ideation' is a Zepbound (weight-management) warning and isn't in Mounjaro's label, so the script must name which label each warning comes from. Low blood sugar: say the higher risk applies only with diabetes plus insulin or a sulfonylurea, in the spoken line too. Kidney injury, severe allergic reactions and aspiration come from post-marketing reports and have no trial rates, so say 'no rate' rather than making one up. This keeps the 'How rare?' title honest. Pancreatitis: give 0.23 vs 0.11 per 100 years only next to the weight-trial 0.14 vs 0.15. Use a real Medication Guide URL, with its revised date, separate from the PI. Never say 'new' about NAION.

pieces.topic: Dropped your tirzepatide single-dose pen, or it looks damaged: what the Instructions for Use say, and what to do if you're unsure
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'Dropped your tirzepatide pen? Here's what the pen guide says.' Quote or paraphrase only the IFU's damage wording that you confirm in the loaded Zepbound and Mounjaro single-dose pen IFUs, each with its own URL and revised date. If neither IFU loads, give no sourced IFU claim. Use only the untagged line 'Not sure it's OK? Don't use it. Ask your pharmacist or call the number in your leaflet.' Don't cite the PI storage section for damage. Keep the scope card 'US single-dose pen; KwikPens and vials have their own leaflets.' Close: 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.', then the loop line.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Pen Dropped on the Floor: Still OK? #shorts
pieces.why: Visible pen moment for the 08:00 slot, matching the winning pen Shorts (pen blood 170, 888 on TikTok). A new moment not covered in the last 30 days. | fact-check: It's useful and safe as long as it doesn't over-claim. Two risks. (1) I'm not confident the US single-dose pen IFU talks about 'dropped' pens at all. Its usual wording is about not using a pen that looks damaged, frozen, or has cloudy or particle-containing medicine. Never put 'dropped' in the IFU's mouth unless the loaded IFU actually says it. (2) The planned fallback won't work. The PI's How Supplied/Storage section (Zepbound PI, 28 Aug 2026) covers storage and temperature, not damage. Citing it for a 'damaged pen' paraphrase would tag a line to a source that doesn't say it. The search keyword 'tirzepatide pen' covers both brands, so cite Mounjaro's single-dose pen IFU too. No sourcing of replacement pens and no dose or missed-dose talk.

pieces.topic: Stomach pain on tirzepatide: ordinary queasy discomfort vs the label's call-right-away signs (pancreatitis and gallbladder wording)
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'Stomach ache on tirzepatide: normal, or a call-right-away sign?' Relief fact in the same sentence: in the trials, GI effects like nausea and stomach discomfort were common, mostly during dose escalation, and decreased over time. Signs, one line each: (1) Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, sometimes felt from the stomach to the back: stop using it and call your healthcare provider right away. (2) Pain in the upper stomach, fever, yellow skin or eyes, or clay-colored stools: call your healthcare provider right away. Then 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.' Then 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.', then the loop line. Show all of these on screen.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide Stomach Pain: Normal or Call Now? #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. A felt symptom that rides the safety-search surge, framed as calm relief plus a clear action. | fact-check: This is a strong, useful safety Short built on label wording. One fix: the gallbladder action in the angle drops 'right away'. The Medication Guide says to call your healthcare provider right away for gallbladder symptoms too, and our rules keep 'right away' and 'healthcare provider' word for word. Only the pancreatitis sign carries 'stop using'. That's label wording, so it's allowed, but keep it attached to that sign only. Don't promise that ordinary discomfort is 'normal' for this viewer. Use the label's hedge: GI effects were common, 'mostly during dose escalation and decreased over time'. One number per sentence at most. The working title is fine.

pieces.topic: Thanksgiving plate on tirzepatide: does eating the turkey and vegetables before the carbs matter? Eating order and your body's own GLP-1
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'On tirzepatide, should you eat the turkey before the stuffing?' By 6 s: 'In one small study of 16 adults with type 2 diabetes, eating protein and vegetables before carbs was linked to smaller blood sugar rises and a higher GLP-1 response after the meal.' One rounded number at most. Then: it's a habit that may help, not a replacement for the medicine, and no tirzepatide trial tested it. As a separate sentence with no 'so': tirzepatide reduces appetite and food intake. Two untagged tips at most: start with the protein you enjoy, then whatever else you like; go back if you're still hungry. Low blood sugar line: if you have diabetes and take insulin or a sulfonylurea, ask your prescriber about the holiday meal. Close: 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.', then the loop line.
pieces.why: Thanksgiving peaks Nov 25–27. A fresh holiday-table angle (eating order and natural GLP-1) that avoids the full-fast, heartburn, drinks, greasy and leftovers Shorts already run. | fact-check: I confirmed the study: Shukla et al., BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care 2017 (PMID 28989726), a randomised crossover in 16 adults with type 2 diabetes. When carbohydrate came last (eaten 10 min after protein and vegetables), glucose iAUC was 53% lower and peaks 54% lower, insulin was lower and GLP-1 excursions were higher than when carbohydrate came first. That's one meal on test days, in people not on tirzepatide. The GLP-1 finding is from type 2 diabetes only. Don't extend it to prediabetes unless you cite a separate study that measured GLP-1 there. Timing: Thanksgiving is 26 Nov 2026, so it must go out before then, with no dates or 'this year' in the narration. The 'Thanksgiving long video' target must actually be live. If it isn't, point to How It Works. No guilt, no calorie talk, no 'bad' foods.
